gloss: set apart as God's, holy; consecrate; sanctuary
summary: קדש marks what is set apart to God, his and taken out of common use. Scripture defines it by its opposite: the priests are to separate “between the holy and the common (חֹל)”, as between unclean and clean (Lev 10:10), and Yahweh, who is holy, separates Israel from the peoples to be his (Lev 20:26). Yahweh is the Holy One; people, places, times and things are holy as his: the Sabbath and his appointed times are proclaimed as מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ, “a holy convocation” (Lev 23), and the מִקְדָּשׁ is the sanctuary where he dwells among them. The verb sets apart, consecrates, or treats as holy; קָדֵשׁ and קְדֵשָׁה name a man or woman dedicated to another god's cult, whom scripture sets beside the harlot and forbids. Ugaritic, Phoenician, Akkadian, Arabic and Ge'ez use the root for holy, consecrate and sanctuary (Akkadian and Arabic also for pure), and Akkadian and Ugaritic name a cult-dedicated woman with it.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh grounds his call on what he is: “You shall be holy, for I, Yahweh your God, am holy” (Lev 19:2; Lev 11:44–45). The holiness is a belonging: “you shall be holy to me, for I Yahweh am holy, and I have separated you from the peoples to be mine” (Lev 20:26); he chose Israel out of all peoples as a people holy to him (Deu 7:6), a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exo 19:6). It is both his act and their keeping: “consecrate yourselves and be holy … keep my statutes and do them; I am Yahweh who makes you holy” (Lev 20:7–8). Peter gives the same command to those called in Christ: “as he who called you is holy, be holy in all your conduct, because it is written, Be holy, for I am holy” (1Pe 1:15–16), and calls them by Exodus's words a holy people (1Pe 2:9). Paul names it God's will and sets it against impurity: “this is God's will, your holiness, that you be separated from all fornication … God did not call you to uncleanness but to holiness” (1Th 4:3, 7). So holiness is not first a feeling or a degree of goodness but belonging to Yahweh, shown by living apart from what he calls unclean.

The one who makes holy is Yahweh: מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם, “who makes you holy”, is how he names himself over Israel and its priests (Exo 31:13; Lev 20:8; Lev 21:8; Lev 22:32), and the nations will know it when his sanctuary is in their midst forever (Ezk 37:28). The priests were made holy by the blood from the altar and the anointing oil sprinkled on them (Exo 29:21; Lev 8:30), and whatever touched the most holy altar became holy (Exo 29:37); Jesus says it is the altar that sanctifies the gift (Mat 23:19). Jesus says the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world (Jhn 10:36), and before his death he prays, “Father, sanctify them in your truth … for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (Jhn 17:17–19). Hebrews says that by God's will “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus the Messiah once” (Heb 10:10), that Jesus suffered outside the city to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb 13:12), and that the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one, so he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11). What the altar and the blood did for the priests, scripture says Christ does for his people by his own offering.

Yahweh is holy beyond comparison: “Holy, holy, holy is Yahweh of hosts” (Isa 6:3), which the living creatures say without rest (Rev 4:8); “none is holy like Yahweh” (1Sa 2:2). He is “God and not man, the Holy One in your midst”, and for that reason does not come to destroy Ephraim (Hos 11:9). He will be shown holy among those who come near him (Lev 10:3), and Moses and Aaron were kept from bringing Israel into the land because they did not trust him, “to treat me as holy before the eyes of the sons of Israel” (Num 20:12). His name, profaned among the nations by Israel, he will sanctify himself by gathering them, cleansing them and giving them a new spirit (Ezk 36:23–27); Jesus teaches his disciples to pray, “may your name be hallowed” (Mat 6:9). Isaiah says, “Yahweh of hosts, him you shall regard as holy; let him be your fear and your dread” (Isa 8:13), and Peter, taking up those words, writes in the Peshitta “sanctify the Lord Messiah in your hearts” (1Pe 3:15): he gives to the Messiah the holiness Isaiah gives to Yahweh of hosts.

God set the seventh day apart at creation because on it he rested from his work (Gen 2:3), and Israel is to remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy, doing no work in it (Exo 20:8–11). Yahweh's appointed times, מוֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה, are holy convocations, מִקְרָאֵי קֹדֶשׁ, which Israel is to proclaim, and he calls them “my appointed times” (Lev 23:2, 4, 37): the weekly Sabbath (Lev 23:3); the first and seventh days of חַג הַמַּצּוֹת, from the fifteenth of the first month after the פֶּסַח (Lev 23:5–8); the fiftieth day counted from the omer (Lev 23:15–21); the first of the seventh month, a memorial of teruah (Lev 23:24); יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים on the tenth (Lev 23:27); and the first and eighth days of חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת from the fifteenth (Lev 23:34–36). On each, no ordinary work is done. The returned exiles kept “all the consecrated appointed times of Yahweh” (Ezr 3:5). A holy day is a day of joy: when the people wept on the first of the seventh month at hearing the law, they were told, “This day is holy to Yahweh your God; do not mourn or weep … the joy of Yahweh is your strength” (Neh 8:2, 9–11). The Sabbath is a sign “that you may know that I am Yahweh who makes you holy” (Exo 31:13; Ezk 20:12), and Isaiah calls it a delight, “the holy of Yahweh, honoured” (Isa 58:13). The times are holy because they are Yahweh's: he sets them apart, and his people meet him in them.

The sanctuary exists so that Yahweh may dwell among his people: “let them make me a מִקְדָּשׁ, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exo 25:8). He promises to set his dwelling among them and walk among them, to be their God and they his people (Lev 26:11–12), and Israel is to keep his Sabbaths and fear his sanctuary (Lev 26:2). When they were scattered he was himself “a little sanctuary” to them in the lands (Ezk 11:16), and he promised a covenant of peace, with his sanctuary in their midst forever, so that the nations would know that he is Yahweh who makes Israel holy (Ezk 37:26–28). To those who regard him as holy he is a sanctuary, but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling (Isa 8:13–14). Paul quotes the promise to the church: “you are the temple of the living God, as it is said, I will dwell among them and walk among them” (2Co 6:16), and draws from it, “let us cleanse ourselves from all impurity of flesh and spirit, and work holiness in the fear of God” (2Co 7:1). Hebrews says the Messiah entered not a sanctuary made by hands but heaven itself, once, with his own blood (Heb 9:12, 24).

BDB files two verb tokens under no stem: Ezk 7:24 מְקַדְשֵׁיהֶם (read here as “their sanctuaries”, מִקְדָּשׁ) and 2Ch 15:18 קָדָשָׁיו (the noun קֹדֶשׁ); they are not given a stem. Verse references are in the Hebrew numbering (Num 17:2–3 = Eng 16:37–38; 1Sa 21:5–6 = Eng 21:4–5; Psa 89:6, 8 = Eng 89:5, 7; Psa 51:13 = Eng 51:11; Dan 4:5–20 = Eng 4:8–23).

Open questions for review: (1) Gloss: “set apart as God's” is taken from scripture's use (Lev 10:10, holy against common; Lev 20:26, holy because separated to be his; Num 16:5, “who is his and who is holy”). No cognate checked shows “separate”: they give holy, consecrate, sanctuary, and in Akkadian and Arabic also pure. The only “far away” sense is Lane's قَدَسَ فِى الأَرْضِ, offered by a commentator as the source of “declare God far removed from impurity”; it is recorded on ar-qadusa and not relied on. (2) Pure: scripture keeps holy/common apart from clean/unclean (Lev 10:10), so “pure” is not taken as the root's core; the hithpael “purify oneself” (2Sa 11:4; Isa 66:17) is the one Hebrew use that matches Akkadian qadāšu, and akk-qadashu is named only there and on the piel “prepare the people”. (3) קָדֵשׁ/קְדֵשָׁה: kept as a word of the root (dedicated to a god), with Akkadian qadištu and Ugaritic qdšt as cognates of the same formation. That the role was harlotry rests on scripture's parallels with זוֹנָה (Gen 38:15, 21; Hos 4:14; Deu 23:18–19); neither cognate source checked says so. Review the gloss “cult prostitute”. (4) Peshitta 1Pe 3:15 reads “the Lord Messiah”, the Textus Receptus κύριον τὸν θεόν; the doctrine follows the Peshitta's wording and says so. (5) Doctrine on holy times gives Lev 23 in the text's own terms; whether to add the New Testament's words on feasts and Sabbaths (Col 2:16–17; Heb 4:9) is left for the user's direction. (6) Arabic مَقْدِس occurs in Lane only in the name of Jerusalem, and Sabaic qds is attested in Biella (p. 447) only in sixth-century Christian inscriptions (“Holy Spirit”, “hold Mass”); either may carry Jewish or Christian usage. Sabaic is not entered as a cognate.
